description:
We are Team SARIS, six undergraduate students from Brazil and Pakistan: Erik, Patrick, Luiz, Renan, Bilal and Bisman. 

As a team, we bring skills in:

Software Development: Python, JavaScript and web technologies to build working tools.

Data Processing & Analysis: handling large datasets and finding meaningful patterns in them.

Visualization & UI/UX: turning raw radar imagery into an analysis visualization.

Our goal is to make SAR data accessible and engaging.
summary: NISAR 3D Observatory is a geo-spatial web-site platform that is created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Dancing with the SARs.” This is a platform intended to monitor the changes in Earth's surface dynamics. NISAR 3D Observatory works with CesiumJS, NASADEM Elevation Data, and Nasa GIBS Imagery and combines a decade of high-resolution history of NISAR L-band SAR with OPERA C-band SAR, while GPM IMERG provides weather data. Furthermore, the importance of the project lies in transforming NASA’s cloud-penetrating satellite raw data into an accessible, transparent and interactive 3D platform using a machine-learning AI, which simplifies technical data for better laymen users' understanding. With the help of monitoring the shifts of radar signals in an Amazon test site and correlation with rainfall, users get the chance to analyze surface dynamics visually using only scientifically proven methods of signal changes detection. As well, as long as there is satellite area coverage, the concept of the platform can be applied to other regions, demonstrating its global significance.
details:
SARIS: Radar Sees the Amazon Change. Do We Know Why?

Every few days a radar satellite passes over the Amazon, through clouds, smoke and darkness, and records how the ground echoes back. Somewhere in those numbers a forest is being cleared, a floodplain is rising, a field is drying out. But a radar image is just a grid of numbers. It shows that something changed, not what or why. Most people who care about the answer (journalists, local governments, students, researchers outside remote sensing) will never open a raw SAR file. SARIS turns that echo into a story anyone can read, and stays honest about what the data can and cannot say.

What is SARIS?

SARIS is an interactive 3D observatory of surface change over South America, with the Amazon at its center. It brings together NASA's newest radar mission, NISAR (L-band), a decade of OPERA RTC-S1 (Sentinel-1, C-band, 2016 to 2026) and NASA climate data on one map.

Pick any point. Choose a period. SARIS finds every radar scene that covers it, reads only the few pixels you need straight from NASA's archives, cleans them and streams back a time series of radar backscatter, side by side with the rain that fell before each pass. Then it tells you what is normal for that place, what is not, and what the next years may look like.

It has three parts:

- The Mission Brief, a narrated presentation that teaches, step by step, how a radar works, what a change in decibels means and why each driver of change leaves its own signature.

- The Observatory, the 3D map: NASA layers, live radar analysis, a forecast to 2030, risks and disaster simulations.

- Data and Methods, a technical record of every data product, model, test and limit, linked from the map.

Features

A 3D observatory

The map shows the real relief of South America with 10 m Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery, 3D buildings in the cities and NASA GIBS layers: NISAR backscatter, surface water, vegetation loss alerts and rain rate. A timeline runs from 2016 to 2030, from C-band history to L-band today to labeled future scenarios.

Live radar

Nothing is preloaded. When you press "Analyze", our backend searches the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) archive, reads only the pixels around your point from each NISAR or OPERA scene, cleans them and streams the rows back live as each scene finishes. The sensor is chosen by the period: NISAR when all of it is from October 2025 on (subject to change depending on local NISAR coverage), otherwise OPERA. Daily rain from GPM IMERG arrives in the same stream.

Rain beside every echo

Wet soil and wet leaves reflect more radar energy. A sudden drop or jump can be rain, not a change on the ground. That is why every radar series is shown next to the rain that fell before each acquisition, so an unusual reading can be checked against the weather before anyone draws a conclusion.

Forecast, risks and what-ifs

For any point, SARIS learns its history since 2016 and projects radar backscatter and rain to 2030 with an uncertainty band, and shows whether it beats a simple "same as last year" rule. It then lists four risks (vegetation loss, flood, drought and fire, unusual change) with level and evidence. Natural disaster simulations (earthquake, flood, wildfire, storm) let you see damage zones grow on the map, clearly labeled as simulations.

Ask the map

An AI bar takes commands in English, Portuguese or Spanish. Open questions are answered only from what the map is showing.

For everyone, in three languages

English, Portuguese and Spanish throughout the decks, the map and the technical record.

---

How the Intelligence Works

We use machine learning where it helps someone understand a place, and we label every output for what it is.

The Decisive Difference: Honest About Cause

Radar says that something changed, not why. Many tools stop at a red pixel and leave the viewer to guess. SARIS does the opposite. It matches each pattern and polarization to a physical driver as a hypothesis, shows the rain that could explain it, tells you the confidence of every reading (high, limited or insufficient) and says plainly when there is too little data. Scenarios never show real imagery. Simulations are labeled as simulations. Every limit we know of is written down in Data and Methods.

We believe a tool that is trusted is worth more than a tool that is impressive.

Our Data

- NISAR GCOV (L-band, HH and HV), from October 2025, via ASF

- OPERA RTC-S1 (Sentinel-1, C-band, VV and VH), 2016 to now, via ASF

- GPM IMERG daily rain, via NASA GES DISC

- NASA GIBS layers: surface water, vegetation loss, rain rate, land surface temperature, soil moisture

- NASA Blue Marble for the 3D Earth

- Supporting data: Sentinel-2 cloudless (EOX), Open-Meteo winds, AWS Terrain Tiles, OpenStreetMap

Built With

React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and three.js on the front end. Python, scikit-learn and a streaming HTTP API (Server-Sent Events) on the back end.

Our Mission: Make Radar Readable

NISAR will map almost all of the Earth's land and ice every 12 days, in any weather, day or night. That is an extraordinary amount of truth about our planet, and today almost nobody outside a lab can read it. SARIS was built on one conviction: showing the health of our planet to all that don't have the know-how to analyze the raw data.
